items.summary: This chapter develops the research programme of Generative Relational Economics (GRE) by translating the conceptual, methodological, and substantive architectures developed earlier in the book into a cumulative, contestable, and revisable programme of inquiry. Its principal concern is answerability: GRE claims should specify what is being investigated, what kinds of evidence can support them, what would count against them, which methods are appropriate to their objects, and under what conditions their scope, formulation, or status should change. The chapter first distinguishes the epistemic status of GRE claims and establishes a modular research architecture. It then formulates research programmes for relational economic structures, allocation, heterogeneous value, value conversion and circulation, generative return, generative spacetime, fast–slow dynamics, economic power, justice, generative exploitation, epistemic economy, and AI-mediated capability asymmetry. These substantive programmes are complemented by domain studies, formal modelling, historical and interpretive inquiry, quantitative and empirical research, comparative theory, institutional experimentation, measurement analysis, counterevidence, negative results, replication, reinterpretation, and research infrastructure. A recurring concern is to prevent operationalization from collapsing the distinctions that motivate GRE. Measurement is therefore treated as a transformation with possible loss and reflexive effects; formalization is treated as task-relative rather than as evidence of ontological commitment; justice research keeps normative premises explicit; power and exploitation require mechanism-level identification rather than inference from asymmetry alone; and cross-domain translation preserves non-equivalence and domain-specific remainders. Failed models, failed translations, null results, counterexamples, and negative evidence are treated as constitutive resources for cumulative research rather than as residuals to be discarded. The chapter concludes by specifying how GRE may interact with neighboring Generative Relational domains while retaining disciplinary containment. Candidate cross-domain structures remain hypotheses for further inquiry rather than presumptive components of a completed general theory. GRE thereby emerges not as a closed theoretical system, but as an open research programme whose concepts, methods, models, and domain claims remain historically situated, empirically answerable, formally inspectable, and institutionally revisable.
items.title: Generative Relational Economics - Chapter 22: Research Programme of Generative Relational Economics

items.summary: Sunnycode v1 provides an open-access computational framework and reproducibility package supporting the research article Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization for Resilient Urban LoRaWAN Networks , submitted to Digital Communications and Networks. The framework integrates OpenStreetMap (OSM) building-level sensing demand, radio-frequency (RF) feasibility, capacity-aware gateway assignment, worst-case single-gateway failure retention (N−1), gateway-load fairness, and road-constrained Steiner backbone synthesis. The repository includes Python implementations of the proposed optimization approach and four independent benchmark methods (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Greedy, and Random Search). Dataset and experimental scope The computational experiment considers 685 building-level sensor anchors, 169 road vertices, 195 street edges, and 89 gateway candidates. The Full benchmark comprises 4,000 run-level observations obtained from 100 repetitions for each combination of five optimization methods and eight gateway budgets (k = 3–10). Repository contents Python source code and computational validation utilities. Nine original CSV files containing experimental observations, aggregated statistics, evaluation effort, and optimizer provenance. OpenStreetMap territorial input ( sunny3.osm ). Forty scientific figures in PDF format. Installation and execution instructions using Anaconda. SHA-256 file-integrity manifest and licensing information. The archived results support independent verification of the reported statistics and new computational experiments. The original historical environment metadata and detailed event histories are not included; therefore, bit-for-bit replay of the historical execution environment is not claimed. Scientific scope: RF coverage and packet delivery ratio are model-derived planning estimates rather than field-calibrated measurements. N−1 resilience represents gateway-access service retention and does not certify fault-tolerant physical-backbone connectivity. This software and dataset are released to support transparent computational research, independent assessment, and further development of resilient urban Internet of Things infrastructure planning.
items.title: Sunnycode v1 A Reproducible Framework for Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization in Urban LoRaWAN Networks

items.summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).
items.title: Extracting Reproducibility Metadata from Machine-Learning Papers: a Taxonomy of Silent Errors and the Cost of Human Verification

items.summary: Code and text-free reproducibility artifacts for the manuscript “Saudi Arabic Automatic Speech Recognition and Dialect Identification Using Calibrated System Combination and Gated Multimodal Fusion,” currently under revision at Scientific Reports . The repository implements a Saudi Arabic automatic speech recognition framework using XLSR-53, XLS-R 300M, XLS-R 1B, and MMS-1B with validation-tuned KenLM decoding, evaluation under a dialect-normalized scoring convention applied to both references and hypotheses, and calibrated N-best system combination. The reproduced combined test WER is 32.49% , compared with 34.04% for the best single-model configuration. XLSR-53 was evaluated on a 1,652-utterance subset of the test set and is therefore treated as an indicative baseline. The repository also provides SaudiDID-X, a multimodal Saudi dialect identification framework using frozen multi-layer MMS-1B acoustic representations and frozen SaudiBERT text features with a residual adapter and gated fusion. The audio-only comparison is the acoustic branch of the same SaudiDID-X training run , not an independently trained model. The archived test macro-F1 values are 52.01% for the audio-only branch and 53.79% for SaudiDID-X. The release includes analysis and reference-training notebooks, configuration metadata, anonymized split identifiers, text-free per-utterance result artifacts, statistical-test outputs, figures, tables, checksums, and a verification script. Raw audio and third-party transcriptions are not redistributed because of source-specific licensing restrictions. v1.0.2: Documentation, provenance, and configuration-metadata corrections. Archived predictions, primary reported metrics, data splits, checksums, and computational implementation are unchanged. See CHANGELOG.md for the complete list of corrections. v1.0.1: Configuration-metadata corrections for the single-run reporting protocol and per-stage training hyperparameters. No result values changed.
items.title: SaudiArabic-ASR-DID: Multi-Model ASR and Multimodal Dialect Identification for Saudi Arabic

items.summary: This reproducibility package accompanies the article “Decomposing cross-study disagreement in renewable-energy priorities: a provenance-preserving typed RASS framework for Türkiye”. It contains the machine-readable source registry, source-extracted numerical tables with article-level provenance, typed records, configuration and policy files, Python analysis code, tests, computational certificates, derived outputs, and figure and table source assets supporting the reported analyses. The package supports source-native replication audits of four published Türkiye renewable-energy prioritization studies; controlled representation and operator experiments; ordinal and numerical evidence synthesis; weight–ontology–missingness robustness analyses; and theorem-certificate checks. Copyrighted publisher PDF files are not included. The source articles are identified through their bibliographic information and DOIs in the source registry. No personal or sensitive data are included. Version 1.0. Usage and reproduction instructions are provided in README.md, and file integrity information is provided in SHA256SUMS.txt.
items.title: Reproducibility data and code for Decomposing cross-study disagreement in renewable-energy priorities: a provenance-preserving typed RASS framework for Türkiye

items.summary: CORE-LLM-Bench is a controlled neurosymbolic benchmark for evaluating ontology-grounded reasoning in large language models. Version 1.1.0 contains 9,048 unique question-hop instances derived from four ontology datasets: Family, Pizza 100, Pizza 250, and OWL2Bench. The benchmark contains 6,032 binary question-answering (BQA) instances and 3,016 open-ended question-answering (OEQA) instances. Benchmark instances support 1-hop and 2-hop ontology contexts and aligned natural-language (NL), formal-symbolic (FS), and entity-abstracted (AR) representations. Ground-truth answers and explanation structures are derived using symbolic ontology reasoning, enabling controlled evaluation according to task formulation, representation, semantic abstraction, context depth, explanation-based reasoning complexity, and reasoning type. The release includes benchmark data, reasoning metadata, provenance and licensing documentation, release manifests and checksums, and scripts supporting benchmark generation, validation, Hugging Face export, and reproducibility. The canonical source-code release is CORE-LLM-Bench v1.1.0 on GitHub. Licensing is component-specific. Repository software is MIT licensed; separable original CORE-LLM-Bench benchmark content is CC BY 4.0; Pizza-derived material follows CC BY 3.0; OWL2Bench-derived material follows Apache-2.0; and Family/FHKB-derived material follows CC BY-SA 3.0. See NOTICE.md for detailed provenance, attribution, and modification information.
items.title: CORE-LLM-Bench: A Controlled Neurosymbolic Benchmark for Ontology-Grounded Reasoning in Large Language Models

items.summary: Replication package for the journal article on attributing LLM-paraphrased source code to the model that produced it, in the setting where someone has an LLM rewrite code that another person wrote so that it no longer looks copied. Contents: the corpus of 144,958 paraphrase pairs (22,053 human-written files in Python, C, C++, Java, C#, Go and PHP, rewritten by Gemini 3 Flash, GPT 5 Nano, Claude 3 Haiku, Qwen 3 Coder 30B, DeepSeek V3.2, Grok 4 Fast and Devstral 2512 under the paraphrasing instruction of Park et al., 2025), the deterministic fold assignment, the 105-feature matrix, the cross-prompt corpus (the same 1,050 files rewritten under two further instructions), 2,400 human revisions of source files from MIT-licensed repositories (the negative set of the paired detection experiment), the out-of-fold outputs of every view and baseline (tree learners, TF-IDF views, fine-tuned CodeBERT and CodeT5 encoders, attention classifier, LPcodedec replication), every result file behind the article's tables and figures, the Colab notebooks for the GPU baselines, and the scripts that rebuild the corpus, run every experiment and regenerate every table and figure. The human-written files come from public repositories under the MIT, Apache 2.0, BSD 2-Clause and BSD 3-Clause licences and are redistributed under those licences with their notices preserved. Personal markers in identifiers were anonymised. The scripts are released under the MIT licence. The LPcode benchmark and the LPcodedec code of Park et al. are not redistributed; the README documents how to obtain them.
items.title: STACAD: replication package for 'Attributing paraphrased source code to the large language model that rewrote it'

items.summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist [Data set]. Kaggle. https://doi.org/10.34740/KAGGLE/DSV/195341 Official source: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/olistbr/brazilian-ecommerce License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (`CC BY-NC-SA 4.0`).
items.title: Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB)

items.summary: This dataset contains the experimental materials and retained research records supporting the master’s thesis on evaluating LLM-based identification of non-functional requirements (NFRs) from agile user stories. The dataset consists of two Excel files: Research_Experiment_Data_Final.xlsx This file contains the retained experimental records used in the study, including: reconstructed user stories and their provenance; human analyst NFR annotations; consensus voting and the resulting baseline NFRs; AI-generated NFR identification results from repeated GPT-4o-mini runs; AI consistency results across repeated runs; AI-human matching and adjudication results; timing observations for human and AI-based NFR identification; System Usability Scale (SUS) responses; per-evaluator and aggregate performance metrics, including precision, recall, and F1-score. 25_reconstructed_stories_.xlsx This file contains the 25 reconstructed user stories used as the experimental input dataset. It documents the source material used for reconstruction, source URLs, source evidence, the rationale for reconstruction, and the resulting reconstructed user stories. The reconstructed stories were created for the experiment and should not be interpreted as verbatim quotations of the original source datasets. Together, these files provide the underlying experimental records and input materials necessary to understand and reproduce the quantitative analyses reported in the thesis. The dataset supports examination of human versus LLM-based NFR identification, including identification accuracy, consistency, agreement with the human-derived baseline, processing time, and usability. The data are provided for research transparency, reproducibility, and further academic analysis. Source publications referenced within the dataset remain the property of their respective copyright holders. The reconstructed user stories are experimental research materials derived from source-supported characteristics and are explicitly documented as reconstructed rather than presented as original source text.
items.title: LLM-Based NFR Identification: Experimental Dataset

items.summary: gpbiometricspy is the Python counterpart of gpbiometrics, with gpbiometrics 2.0.0 frozen as its initial semantic reference. items.summary: Abstract   The Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII) is a retrospective analytical methodology designed to reconstruct, in a traceable and auditable manner, the probable pathway leading from an initial problem or question to a completed scientific product. This manual brings together the universal prompt, a mandatory common core, ten core modules—including bibliographic analysis (SUII-B)—and six specialised extensions: journalistic and opinion texts (SUII-P), audiovisual or audio documents (SUII-AV), legislation and regulatory documents (SUII-L), case law and judicial decisions (SUII-J), critical appraisal of scientific articles (SUII-LC), and traceable research information management for datasets and research data objects (SUII-TRIM). Each module guides the extraction of locatable traces, classification of the epistemic status of claims, and construction of matrices linking evidence, inference, confidence, alternatives, and required verification. SUII-TRIM extends this logic to the provenance, versioning, transformation, quality control, preservation, access, and reuse of research datasets, while preserving the distinction between directly observed information, information provided by the researcher, reasoned inference, and non-determinable information. The method separates retrospective reconstruction from the prospective generation of hypotheses and requires rival explanations whenever the evidence does not support a unique conclusion. It also incorporates procedures for methodological auditing, version comparison, conceptual genealogy, peer review, algorithmic-bias assessment, external validation, teaching, and traceable research data management. SUII is not intended to recover the authors’ actual psychological history or to replace validated tools for methodological appraisal, risk-of-bias assessment, certainty of evidence, data stewardship, or repository curation. Its application requires version-controlled corpora, decision logs, retention of prompts and outputs, source verification, preservation of original data objects when applicable, and mandatory human oversight. When the available traces are insufficient, the appropriate result is “not determinable.” The manual provides practical criteria for selecting, combining, and quality-controlling the modules according to the product under analysis and the research objective, while maintaining explicit boundaries between documented evidence, reasoned inference, speculation, and unresolved uncertainty .   Resumen   El Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII) es una metodología de análisis retrospectivo orientada a reconstruir, de forma trazable y auditable, el itinerario probable que conduce desde un problema o pregunta inicial hasta un producto científico finalizado. Este manual reúne el prompt universal, un núcleo común obligatorio, diez módulos nucleares y seis extensiones especializadas: análisis bibliográfico (SUII-B), textos periodísticos y de opinión (SUII-P), documentos audiovisuales o sonoros (SUII-AV), legislación y normativa (SUII-L), jurisprudencia y sentencias (SUII-J), lectura crítica de artículos científicos (SUII-LC) y gestión trazable de información y datos de investigación (SUII-TRIM). Cada módulo guía la extracción de huellas localizables, la clasificación del estado epistemológico de las afirmaciones y la construcción de matrices que relacionan evidencia, inferencia, confianza, alternativas y comprobaciones necesarias. El método separa la reconstrucción retrospectiva de la generación prospectiva de hipótesis y exige formular explicaciones rivales cuando la evidencia no permite una conclusión única. Asimismo, incorpora procedimientos para auditoría me

items.summary: Calibration of RG-6 Coaxial Cables for Shear and Tensile Displacement Measurement Using Time Domain Reflectometry and a Causal Ordered State Estimator.” The archive contains the complete Python analysis code, publication figure scripts, distance-resolved waveform profiles, zero-displacement waveform points, benchmark-model outputs, ordered-state predictions, posterior state probabilities, state-emission templates, transition matrices, negative-control results, run configuration files, editable vector figures, software requirements and file-integrity checksums. The prediction target is the recorded applied displacement in millimetres. The measured unloaded impedance of 88.4 Ω is retained as the experimental zero-displacement reference. Shear and tensile loading are evaluated separately using nested Leave One Cable Out validation. Conventional benchmark stability is assessed using three predetermined computational seeds. The ordered state estimator is deterministic for a fixed training fold and selected parameter setting. Target-permutation and observation-order controls are repeated 200 times for each loading mode. The ordered estimator achieved pooled R² values of 0.9898 for shear and 0.9677 for tensile loading. The corresponding MAE values were 0.3222 and 0.2667 mm, while the RMSE values were 0.8756 and 0.5164 mm. These results demonstrate cable-to-cable transfer among nominally identical specimens tested using the same apparatus and controlled monotonic loading protocol. They do not establish generalization to cyclic loading, combined deformation, different installation media, environmental variation or field conditions. Instructions for reproducing the analysis and descriptions of the included files are provided in the README file.
items.title: Code and Results for Calibration of RG-6 Coaxial Cables for Shear and Tensile Displacement Measurement Using Time Domain Reflectometry and a Causal Ordered State Estimator

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23147109 . ## Summary Routing evaluations start the clock too late: they measure serving-time savings but ignore the upfront supervision cost — up to N×M query–model executions before deployment. The paper introduces supervision-amortized metrics: SA-BEP (deployment queries needed for serving savings to recover supervision spend, Eq. 1) and SA-CR (cost ratio after amortizing over horizon H). SaveRouter learns from sparse feedback via query grouping, adaptive capability–uncertainty acquisition (UCB, Eq. 2), a hierarchical group–model capability estimator (two-way additive prior + shrinkage), and a query-level residual correction. On four benchmarks (LLMRouterBench, Mixinstruct, MMR-Bench, RouterBench) it uses only 33–41% of training feedback while matching or beating fully supervised routing quality, cutting break-even volume ~1.9–9.5× vs. the fastest conventional router (e.g., LLMRouterBench: 5.3K vs. 11.5K queries; RouterBench: 42.6K vs. 326.4K). ## Strengths 1. **The economic framing is the contribution, and it's correct.** Eq. 1 makes explicit what practitioners feel but papers ignore: identical serving efficiency can mean wildly different payback if one router cost 10× more to build. The "decision sufficiency vs. matrix recovery" distinction (§3.2) — routing needs argmax[y − λc], not the full quality matrix — is crisp and should change how people budget supervision. Figure 1(b) (EmbedLLM recovers 99% of full-supervision accuracy at 30% supervision) is a genuinely useful empirical fact. 2. **Honest reporting of inconvenient results.** Table 2 shows Random-K reaching break-even *earlier* than SaveRouter (3.8K vs. 5.3K) — reported and correctly interpreted (earliest payback ≠ long-horizon efficiency). Papers that publish the result complicating their story earn trust. 3. **Serious evaluation breadth.** Four heterogeneous benchmarks, ten baselines through one ORBIT pipeline with identical splits, ablations of both estimator and acquisition, a supervision-budget sweep (Figure 3), and paper-derived reimplementations disclosed as such. ## Major concerns 1. **C0 excludes the most expensive cost: labels.** Supervision cost charges only model executions — "router training itself is not included in C0" (Appendix A.1), and per-pair costs come pre-computed from the benchmark. In practice, quality labels for open-ended tasks need LLM judges or humans, and the judging bill often dominates execution. The payback horizons describe a world where labels are free once the model runs; a judge-pricing sensitivity analysis would test whether the 1.9–9.5× advantage survives a real labeling pipeline. 2. **On some benchmarks, the honest conclusion is "don't route."** Mixinstruct needs 1.23M deployment queries for even SaveRouter to break even; on MMR-Bench most methods sit at CR = 1.0000 and SA-BEP = ∞ — never beating the best single model. The paper's own metrics produce this conclusion but never state it. 3. **Acquisition is simulated on a static matrix.** "Adaptive acquisition" reveals entries of a pre-computed matrix under a fixed 20/80 in-domain split (seed 42) — no distribution shift, no model-pool churn, no price changes. But the economic argument is about real deployment, where the common event is a new model joining the pool or a price change invalidating the trade-off. Pool-churn is untested, and the paper has no limitations section at all — a notable absence for deployment-economic claims. ## Practitioner perspective "Will this router ever pay back what it cost to build?" is the question I ask before any routing project, and SA-BEP is a metric I will actually use. But the production C0 includes the judge pipeline, the eval harness, and engineer time — none on this paper's books. My rule of thumb: if projected deployment volume is under ~10× the SA-BEP computed on your own full cost basis, skip the rou
items.title: PREreview of "Routing Should Pay for Itself: Sparse Supervision for Economical LLM Routing"

(2024, Nature) has 87.9 % validation accuracy, tested in Colombia with open data and new code. Verdict: partially supported. items.summary: Replication package for an empirical comparison of the retrieval engines an offline, memory-constrained on-device assistant can embed: SQLite/FTS5, DuckDB-FTS, in-memory BM25, an in-memory linear scan, MiniLM with HNSW on CPU, and the on-disk vector store sqlite-vec. Cost (latency, build time, footprint) and retrieval quality are measured together on WikiText-103, SQuAD, Project Gutenberg and the Turkish TQuAD set, with an embedded hybrid and a coverage-gated router, quantized and ONNX encoders, stronger small encoders, an isolated cost decomposition, a downstream answer-recall check, an incremental-update test, bootstrap confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests. The package holds all code, the result files, the published tables and figures, and two checking scripts: one re-derives every table value from the result files, the other redraws the figures and compares them with the published files. The Gutenberg and SQuAD files are included; TQuAD, whose repository has no license, is downloaded and checked against its SHA-256; the WikiText-103 scaling corpus is a separate file in this record. DATA_MANIFEST.txt lists the SHA-256 of every input. The lexical scaling measurement was repeated on one Android phone; everything else was measured on an x86 workstation, and energy was not measured. Code: MIT. Data: their own licenses (public domain for Gutenberg, CC BY-SA for SQuAD and WikiText-103).

It documents the source material used for reconstruction, source URLs, source evidence, the rationale for reconstruction, and the resulting reconstructed user stories. The reconstructed stories were created for the experiment and should not be interpreted as verbatim quotations of the original source datasets. Together, these files provide the underlying experimental records and input materials necessary to understand and reproduce the quantitative analyses reported in the thesis. The dataset supports examination of human versus LLM-based NFR identification, including identification accuracy, consistency, agreement with the human-derived baseline, processing time, and usability. The data are provided for research transparency, reproducibility, and further academic analysis. Source publications referenced within the dataset remain the property of their respective copyright holders. The reconstructed user stories are experimental research materials derived from source-supported characteristics and are explicitly documented as reconstructed rather than presented as original source text.

items.summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).
items.title: Extracting Reproducibility Metadata from Machine-Learning Papers: a Taxonomy of Silent Errors and the Cost of Human Verification

items.summary: Rank Access and Closure Depth in the Relation-Layer Cohomology of Token Arenas A refuted conjecture, a refuted mechanism, and two species of invariant harmonic residue     Driven by Dean Kulik October 2026     Abstract A K disj -type relation layer over a token arena assigns cohomology to a graph by declaring which closed loops count as relations. We settle an open problem about such layers and then identify what actually governs them. First, the conjecture that two vertex orbits force ε harm ( K 4 ) = 0 is refuted by an exact 12-vertex counterexample with |Aut| = 24, reproduced by two implementations whose constructions of the invariant cochain space share no logic. Second, we localize the failure: it is not a shortage of cells. On the witness's two-dimensional residue, all 1083 arena 4-cycles supply rank 1, while 20 arena 3-cycles of an excluded shape supply rank 2, and the two nonzero square families have the same image, a single line. Third, we refute the natural mechanism for this — that the residue is an odd-cycle blind spot — by exhibiting bipartite arenas, containing no odd cycle of any length, that still carry residue. The operative property is omission from the declared family, not parity. Fourth, we prove that ε harm ( K 3,4 ) > 0 on an infinite family — every cycle graph with n ≥ 5 and 2 ≤ K ≤ n−1, under the trivial group and the rotation subgroup, and zero under the full dihedral group — answering a question the odd-cycle reading had posed. Fifth, we define closure depth L closure , prove it exceeds 4 for every member of that family, and measure it as exactly n for C n and 4 for the witness, so no short vocabulary closes the family. This separates two populated regimes: residue a longer reader dissolves, and residue carried by configuration-space topology. Finally we identify the second kind. At trivial group the framework's own quantity is simplicial H 1 over ℚ , and the declared cells are the 2-skeleton of Abrams' discretized configuration space; the cell counts and Euler characteristic are verified against closed form, Abrams' subdivision hypothesis for C n reduces to n ≥ K + 1, the measured rank is 1 on all 33 admissible rows and 0 on all 8 excluded boundary rows, and the equivariant degree is solved exactly: +1 for rotations, −1 for reflections. All arithmetic is exact rational. Keywords: graph configuration space, graph braid group, token graph, discrete Morse theory, equivariant cohomology, cube complex, relation layer, closure depth MSC 2020: 55R80, 05C10, 20F36, 55N91, 05C85 License: CC BY-NC 4.0. Source code and executed notebook accompany this paper; see Appendix B. 1. Introduction A graph does not come with a cohomology. One is obtained by declaring a relation layer: a set of closed loops in some derived space that are stipulated to bound. Change the declaration and the cohomology changes while the graph does not. This paper is about what that dependence actually is, measured rather than described. The derived space here is a token arena . Fix a finite simple graph X , an integer K ≥ 1, and a group G ≤ Aut( X ). The arena A K ( X ) has the K -element subsets of V ( X ) as vertices, with an edge whenever two subsets differ by moving one token along one edge of X . A relation layer declares a family of arena loops as 2-cells; the G -invariant cochain complex of the resulting 2-complex has a first cohomology whose dimension we write ε harm . The quantity is relative to the declaration, and that is the point. Two declarations are natural and were already in use. K disj admits only commuting squares : two token moves along base edges with disjoint closed supports, which therefore commute. K 4 admits every 4-cycle of the arena. Since K disj ⊆ K 4 , monotonicity gives ε harm ( K 4 ) ≤ ε harm ( K disj ), and the interesting question is when the larger family closes what the smaller one l

items.summary: Code, protocol, and aggregate results for the article When Low Response Does Not Mean No Effect: A Methodological Audit of Response-Derived Weak Supervision for Financial News Kittikorn Takham, Thanayut Changruenngam, Tanaphong Prommai, and Aree Binprathan. FinTech (MDPI), submitted. This release is the version of the repository that accompanies the submitted manuscript. Contents Analysis code ( scripts/ ), unit tests ( tests/ ), and settings ( config.json ) The external-replication protocol, its freeze record, the pre-freeze inspection output, and the deviation log ( research/ ) Every aggregate table and figure behind the article and its supplementary materials ( results/ , figures/ ) Byte-identical originals of the hash-locked files ( archive/ ) Check it without any data python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python tools/verify_release.py python -m unittest discover -s tests verify_release.py checks every file against SHA256SUMS , the replication lock, the provenance snapshots, the code behind each result folder, and the equivalence of the released tables with the original run. Not included Thai news text, price panels, and FNSPID are not redistributed. FNSPID can be downloaded from its authors' repository; the README explains how to regenerate the replication from it. Code released under the MIT License.
